title: Magical Staircase
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later diagrams reviewed. Begin immediately before the illustrated Qxb6+ at 120 seconds, after Qa7+/Kg6, in the complete eight-piece later diagram: White Kb3/Qa7/f4/g4 against Kg6/Rb6/b5/f3. Native48–50 confirm the queen on a7, king route from h7 to g6, and final Qb6 capture from a7. Qxb6+ captures the rook into an exact seven-piece White win, with all b5/f3/f4/g4 pawns retained. The earlier review counted eight pieces after that capture; the actual full final board has seven. Each subsequent Black reply and White response here is an independently supplied representative continuation, with every encoded seven-piece position exactly tablebase checked. The initial eleven-piece zigzag, queen interpositions and all king alternatives before the final fork remain outside this selected conversion proof.
transcript: Many players forget that the chessboard is a pretty big place. In this position, white might seem lost because the knight is pinned to the king and there are two attackers, meaning that black is about to pick it up. The hero playing with white can defend the knight, but the villain can play the brilliant rook takes e6. Now, after taking this rook, this position is headed for a draw where black is going to be the only one playing for a win having an extra pawn, leaving white with the only option to check the black king. Now, importantly, the king cannot go here because now f takes g5 would lead to a checkmate in just a couple of moves. And if the queen covers the check, now knight to f8 would be a fork picking up the queen and winning the game. But of course, the king can simply go to h8 and be safe from the check. But in chess, sometimes you have to trust the position and white has nothing better but to deliver another check. And so, it does exactly that. Now, of course, the queen cannot cover because of checkmate, so the king comes back up. And all of a sudden, white realizes that he has a brilliant idea in this position. In fact, this is one of those very rare situations called staircase, where the queen can deliver a series of checks zigzagging down the board using the forceful checks to force black to move and bringing the queen to a favorable place. Now, after the king goes back, this is when we realize that the a-file and the first rank are completely open. So, the white queen can start delivering checks to the corners like this. But white has a better idea and he comes back to a1, now forcing the king to come out this way because again, the queen cannot cover because of checkmate. And after the king does that, the queen now flies to a8, forcing the king up. But now, we have successfully placed the king and queen in the exact place where we want them to be. And knight to g5 is a fork picking up the queen and after another fork, white is going to very easily win this game. If you love incredible chess, check out Chess Mind AI. In particular, I suggest you check out their Chess GPT quiz. Give it a shot.
